Retrospec Weekender Electric Pump Review – Features, Usability, and Portability
The Retrospec Weekender pump is fast and easy to use with iSUPs and other inflatable items.
The Weekender pump has a standard size and shape with controls on the handle.
Sometimes less is more, and when it comes to getting your board inflated and on the water, a simple pump is just the ticket.
After plugging the Weekender pump into a 12v DC power source (like your car), the unit automatically powers on. The first time you use the Weekender pump you’ll need to set your desired inflation pressure (selectable in either PSI or Bar), but after that the pump will remember the last-used setting.
There are four easy to understand buttons on the pump handle.
The “PSI/BAR” button switches between the two units of measure. The “+” and “–” buttons adjust the pressure setting higher and lower, and the power button activates and deactivates the pump.
The backlit LCD screen is easy to read outdoors, even in bright sunlight, and will automatically turn itself off after two minutes without input or use.
Once you’ve set the desired pressure level on the pump (between 0 – 20 PSI / 0 – 1.38 Bar), simply connect the hose to the pump and board and press the power button to begin inflation. The Weekender pump will automatically turn off once it reaches the desired pressure.
The adapters are connected to the hose with a plastic string and the O-rings come in a separate baggie.
Along with the pump itself, you also get the pump hose, six different valve adapters, and additional O-rings. There are four O-rings with different thicknesses included with the adapters that let you get an exact fit for whichever valve types you are working with.
The different valve adapters and O-rings let you inflate everything from beach balls to paddle boards, kayaks, air mattresses, and more.
There are inflation and deflation ports on the Weekender Pump.
The pump hose attaches easily to the pump body with a rotating collar. Simply screw the hose onto the “inflate” port of the pump when getting ready for the day, and you can use the “deflate” side to finish removing all of the air from your board after initially opening the board valve.
Fully deflating your board with the pump makes it much easier to roll up and fit into the board bag. You will need to monitor the pump when deflating, though, as there is no automatic cutoff when using the pump in reverse.
The large handle is easy to grab, but significantly increases the size of the pump.
The Weekender pump does not come with a storage bag to keep the hose, adapters, and pump together. There is a twist tie for the pump power cable, but no integrated storage.
The handle is easy to grab to move the pump around, but does greatly increase the overall size of the pump body and makes it more difficult to fit into your SUP bag.

An electric pump is one of the best accessories you can purchase for your stand up paddle board. Electric paddle board pumps save you the energy of hand-pumping and help you get on the water faster. Instead of inflating your paddle board by hand and then getting ready to hit the water, you can change clothes, apply sunscreen, fill water bottles, and more all while an electric pump inflates your iSUP.
Electric SUP Pumps are designed specifically for the challenges of inflating a paddle board. They have two stages: a high-flow/low-pressure stage to inflate the board from flat to about 1 PSI and then a low-flow/high-pressure stage that brings your paddle board to its final pressure. Each pump has an automatic cutoff that you can set to your desired pressure. Once the board reaches that pressure, the pump will automatically turn off to prevent over-pressurizing your board.
In the past, electric SUP pumps have required you to connect directly to your car’s battery or plug into a 12v socket (“cigarette lighter”) in your car. But now, many electric pumps with built-in lithium-ion batteries can inflate multiple paddle boards extremely quickly.

Features and Usability:
The Shark III comes with all the bells and whistles you could hope for. The pump itself has, of course, automatic inflation and deflation capabilities and can bring your board up to 20 PSI. It has an onboard active cooling system and a large LCD Display screen. However, like the Cachalot 2S, the screen is difficult to read in bright daylight.
You can control the pump’s settings with the four buttons located on the top of the pump. The screen indicates battery life remaining with color indicators around the edge of the screen. The Shark III also has different settings for inflating SUPs, Kites/Wings, and Air Mattresses, as well as a memory function to recall your preferred settings.
The biggest downside of the Shark III is its size. At 6.5 pounds and with a voluminous shape, it’s hard to forget where you put the pump.
Inflation Speed:
The Shark III takes over the top spot for the fastest electric pump we’ve reviewed, inflating our test board to 15 PSI in an average of 5 minutes.
Battery and Other Accessories:
The internal 74Wh battery has enough juice to reliably inflate three paddle boards. When the battery gets low, you can plug the Shark III into a 12v power source to operate the pump, though it inflates at a much slower speed than with the battery. The USB-C port can also charge your phone and other devices.
Bottom Line: The Outdoor Master Shark 3 is an ultra-fast and versatile rechargeable electric pump.

Features, Usability, and Portability
The iRocker electric pump includes alligator clamps to use with a car battery, spare fuse, and spare o-ring.
The iRocker 12v pump is a great tool for hassle-free inflation of your iSUP. With a maximum pressure of 20 psi and detailed display screen you can use the iRocker 12v pump with just about any iSUP with a standard Halkey-Roberts valve. The cord garage keeps things tidy for storage and the included 12v battery alligator clamp adapter lets you use a 12v battery directly if you do not have an available cigarette lighter style outlet.
While the display has tons of great information (current pressure, set pressure, input voltage, pump stage) the greatest downside of this pump’s usability comes in selecting your pressure. Instead of independent buttons for changing the pressure setting up or down the iRocker 12v pump has only a single button that increases the pressure setting from 0.5-20 psi (selectable in 0.5 psi increments) until it maxes out at 20 psi and restarts at 0.5 psi. So if you are inflating multiple boards with different pressures, it’s best to start with the lower pressure board first so that you don’t have to cycle all the way around just to go from 18 psi to 15 psi for example.
The LCD display has lots of great information, but changing pressure settings is clunky.
While there is only 1 button to change the pressure settings, the iRocker 12v pump has three different buttons to start the pump itself.
“Auto” – which will automatically select the low-pressure stage or high-pressure mode based on the current inflation pressure of the board
“Low” – which only runs the pump in the low-pressure mode (maxing out around 1 psi)
“High” – which only runs the pump in the high-pressure mode (Maxing out at 20 psi)
Selecting the Auto option is usually the best choice in almost any situation. I can honestly say that I’ve never purposefully selected either of the other two functions when inflating boards, and this is the only electric pump I’ve encountered that actually gives users the ability to do so.
I hope that future versions of this pump will replace the “High” and “Low” option buttons with “Pressure +” and “Pressure -” to greatly increase the overall usability of this pump.
The iRocker 12v pump is not the smallest pump we’ve tested, but the boxy, flat form factor makes it very easy to pack into an iSUP bag. The new lineup of compact Ultra series iSUPs from iRocker actually include the electric pump instead of a manual pump. It comes in a neat little carrying bag that fits the pump and all of its accessories. Unfortunately the stand-alone version of this pump does not include a bag, but is still quite easy to pack with your board.
The power cord stores into a small compartment on the side of the pump.

Inflation Speed and Sound
the iRocker electric pump is on the faster side of average among the pumps we’ve tested. While plugged into a constant 12v power source (not a battery) the iRocker 12v pump inflated our medium-sized test board (11’ x 32” x 6”) to 15psi in just over 10 minutes, compared to the 12-15 minute times of many other electric pumps.
When hooked up to a 12v battery pack, the iRocker 12v pump wasn’t quite as fast, but still beat much of the competition with inflation times between 11:40 and 12:15 depending on the input voltage from the battery. Like with all electric pumps, as the voltage from the battery decreases, the inflation times increase.
The tradeoff to this speed is the noise. The iRocker 12v pump was the loudest we tested, chiming in at 82 dB measured at head-height above the pump. Comparatively, our quietest tested pump was 80 dB and the sound of an iSUP deflating measured 89dB.

One of the most common things I see on SUP forums and Facebook groups is…I’ve just bought a paddleboard, it’s the best thing ever, but I really struggled to pump it up to the recommended 15psi. What is the best electric SUP pump to buy…
Almost everyone who’s got an inflatable paddleboard can relate to this, and almost everyone does find it difficult to pump up their board to the maximum pressure. So don’t worry, you aren’t alone here. It’s tiring, can be sweaty work on a hot day and the last few PSI can be really hard to get. I’m 6’2 and 85kgs, and to get up to 17 or 18 PSI I have to put all my effort into pumping, so I can imagine if you’re small and lightweight, it could be impossible to reach that pressure where the board performs at its best.
Whilst it might be slightly quicker and less noisy to inflate a paddleboard with a manual pump, especially if it’s a premium double chamber pump, it is not the easiest way to go about getting on the water.
So the first purchase after getting your paddleboard might well be an electric SUP pump.
Plug the electric paddleboard pump into your 12V lighter socket in your car, attach the hose to the board, turn it on and away you go. Some pumps even have an automatic shut-off function, so you pre-set the PSI you want the paddleboard to inflate to and just let the pump do its thing. Once it hits the PSI you set, it turns off by itself. So no worries about forgetting you turned the pump on whilst you faff around, drink coffee and chat to friends (which I’ve done a few times).
What I love about having an electric paddleboard pump is whilst it’s inflating, you can get yourself ready, assess the conditions and not be knackered before you hit the water.
A word of warning
What I don’t love about electric sup pumps is the noise and it has somewhat split opinions within the paddleboarding community here in the UK. Sure they are easy, but they make a hell of a noise and if you are in a residential area, you can easily piss off the locals. This is especially the case if you want to do a sunrise SUP session at 6:30 am on a Sunday morning!
We’ve had a local paddleboard group shut down recently because residents complained about the noise whilst inflating the boards.
So if you want to use an electric sup pump, please be respectful of where you are using it. If you find you are trying to inflate the board first thing in a built-up area, maybe think twice and try a double chamber pump.
How we ran the test
Along with our usual review of ease of use, quality and price, we also ran a head-to-head test to see what pump what the quickest and which one was the quietest. It was for us to see if there is much variation in the performance of these pumps, or are they just all very similar with a different plastic shell?
We used a Bluefin 12’ Cruise as the test board to inflate. The board is a large all-rounder that can withstand high pressures, so perfect to test these pumps with. For the time we simply used the stopwatch on our phone to record how long it took to get the Bluefin to 15PSI.
For the noise, we used an app called ‘Sound meter’ that records decibels using the mobile phone speaker. The test took place in a quiet area, so hopefully gives a good indication of the noise. We tried to simulate real-world conditions, like placing the pump on the pavement.
It’s by no means a perfect, scientific test, but I think some readers will find the numbers interesting.

Retrospec Weekender Electric Pump Review – Features, Usability, and Portability
The Retrospec Weekender pump is fast and easy to use with iSUPs and other inflatable items.
The Weekender pump has a standard size and shape with controls on the handle.
Sometimes less is more, and when it comes to getting your board inflated and on the water, a simple pump is just the ticket.
After plugging the Weekender pump into a 12v DC power source (like your car), the unit automatically powers on. The first time you use the Weekender pump you’ll need to set your desired inflation pressure (selectable in either PSI or Bar), but after that the pump will remember the last-used setting.
There are four easy to understand buttons on the pump handle.
The “PSI/BAR” button switches between the two units of measure. The “+” and “–” buttons adjust the pressure setting higher and lower, and the power button activates and deactivates the pump.
The backlit LCD screen is easy to read outdoors, even in bright sunlight, and will automatically turn itself off after two minutes without input or use.
Once you’ve set the desired pressure level on the pump (between 0 – 20 PSI / 0 – 1.38 Bar), simply connect the hose to the pump and board and press the power button to begin inflation. The Weekender pump will automatically turn off once it reaches the desired pressure.
The adapters are connected to the hose with a plastic string and the O-rings come in a separate baggie.
Along with the pump itself, you also get the pump hose, six different valve adapters, and additional O-rings. There are four O-rings with different thicknesses included with the adapters that let you get an exact fit for whichever valve types you are working with.
The different valve adapters and O-rings let you inflate everything from beach balls to paddle boards, kayaks, air mattresses, and more.
There are inflation and deflation ports on the Weekender Pump.
The pump hose attaches easily to the pump body with a rotating collar. Simply screw the hose onto the “inflate” port of the pump when getting ready for the day, and you can use the “deflate” side to finish removing all of the air from your board after initially opening the board valve.
Fully deflating your board with the pump makes it much easier to roll up and fit into the board bag. You will need to monitor the pump when deflating, though, as there is no automatic cutoff when using the pump in reverse.
The large handle is easy to grab, but significantly increases the size of the pump.
The Weekender pump does not come with a storage bag to keep the hose, adapters, and pump together. There is a twist tie for the pump power cable, but no integrated storage.
The handle is easy to grab to move the pump around, but does greatly increase the overall size of the pump body and makes it more difficult to fit into your SUP bag.

An electric pump is one of the best accessories you can purchase for your stand up paddle board. Whether it is your first time on a SUP or you are a professional paddle boarder, you can’t beat the hands-free ease of an electric paddle board pump. Electric paddle board pumps save you the energy of hand-pumping and help you get on the water faster. Instead of inflating your paddle board by hand and then getting ready to hit the water, you can change clothes, apply sunscreen, fill water bottles, and more all while an electric pump inflates your iSUP.
Electric SUP Pumps are designed specifically for the challenges of inflating a paddle board. They have two stages: a high-flow/low-pressure stage to inflate the board from flat to about 1 PSI and then a low-flow/high-pressure stage that brings your paddle board to its final pressure. Each pump has an automatic cutoff that you can set to your desired pressure. Once the board reaches that pressure, the pump will automatically turn off to prevent over-pressurizing your board.
In the past, electric SUP pumps have required you to connect directly to your car’s battery or plug into a 12v socket (“cigarette lighter”) in your car. But now, many electric pumps with built-in lithium-ion batteries can inflate multiple paddle boards extremely quickly.

The Shark III comes with all the bells and whistles you could hope for. The pump itself has, of course, automatic inflation and deflation capabilities and can bring your board up to 20 PSI. The biggest downside of the Shark III is its size. At 6.5 pounds and with a voluminous shape, it’s hard to forget where you put the pump.

The internal 74Wh battery has enough juice to reliably inflate three paddle boards. The USB-C port can also charge your phone and other devices.

Features, Usability, and Portability
The iRocker electric pump includes alligator clamps to use with a car battery, spare fuse, and spare o-ring.
The iRocker 12v pump is a great tool for hassle-free inflation of your iSUP. With a maximum pressure of 20 psi and detailed display screen you can use the iRocker 12v pump with just about any iSUP with a standard Halkey-Roberts valve. The cord garage keeps things tidy for storage and the included 12v battery alligator clamp adapter lets you use a 12v battery directly if you do not have an available cigarette lighter style outlet.
While the display has tons of great information (current pressure, set pressure, input voltage, pump stage) the greatest downside of this pump’s usability comes in selecting your pressure. Instead of independent buttons for changing the pressure setting up or down the iRocker 12v pump has only a single button that increases the pressure setting from 0.5-20 psi (selectable in 0.5 psi increments) until it maxes out at 20 psi and restarts at 0.5 psi. So if you are inflating multiple boards with different pressures, it’s best to start with the lower pressure board first so that you don’t have to cycle all the way around just to go from 18 psi to 15 psi for example.
The LCD display has lots of great information, but changing pressure settings is clunky.
While there is only 1 button to change the pressure settings, the iRocker 12v pump has three different buttons to start the pump itself.
“Auto” – which will automatically select the low-pressure stage or high-pressure mode based on the current inflation pressure of the board
“Low” – which only runs the pump in the low-pressure mode (maxing out around 1 psi)
“High” – which only runs the pump in the high-pressure mode (Maxing out at 20 psi)
Selecting the Auto option is usually the best choice in almost any situation. I can honestly say that I’ve never purposefully selected either of the other two functions when inflating boards, and this is the only electric pump I’ve encountered that actually gives users the ability to do so.
I hope that future versions of this pump will replace the “High” and “Low” option buttons with “Pressure +” and “Pressure -” to greatly increase the overall usability of this pump.
The iRocker 12v pump is not the smallest pump we’ve tested, but the boxy, flat form factor makes it very easy to pack into an iSUP bag. The new lineup of compact Ultra series iSUPs from iRocker actually include the electric pump instead of a manual pump. It comes in a neat little carrying bag that fits the pump and all of its accessories. Unfortunately the stand-alone version of this pump does not include a bag, but is still quite easy to pack with your board.
The power cord stores into a small compartment on the side of the pump.

the iRocker electric pump is on the faster side of average among the pumps we’ve tested. When hooked up to a 12v battery pack, the iRocker 12v pump wasn’t quite as fast, but still beat much of the competition with inflation times between 11:40 and 12:15 depending on the input voltage from the battery. Like with all electric pumps, as the voltage from the battery decreases, the inflation times increase.
The tradeoff to this speed is the noise. The iRocker 12v pump was the loudest we tested, chiming in at 82 dB measured at head-height above the pump. Comparatively, our quietest tested pump was 80 dB and the sound of an iSUP deflating measured 89dB.
Every 1 dB increase is roughly a 7% increase in perceived volume. 60 dB is roughly the volume of normal conversation and 90 dB is typically considered the threshold for harmful volume.

One of the most common things I see on SUP forums and Facebook groups is…I’ve just bought a paddleboard, it’s the best thing ever, but I really struggled to pump it up to the recommended 15psi. What is the best electric SUP pump to buy…
Almost everyone who’s got an inflatable paddleboard can relate to this, and almost everyone does find it difficult to pump up their board to the maximum pressure. So don’t worry, you aren’t alone here. It’s tiring, can be sweaty work on a hot day and the last few PSI can be really hard to get. I’m 6’2 and 85kgs, and to get up to 17 or 18 PSI I have to put all my effort into pumping, so I can imagine if you’re small and lightweight, it could be impossible to reach that pressure where the board performs at its best.
Whilst it might be slightly quicker and less noisy to inflate a paddleboard with a manual pump, especially if it’s a premium double chamber pump, it is not the easiest way to go about getting on the water.
So the first purchase after getting your paddleboard might well be an electric SUP pump.
Plug the electric paddleboard pump into your 12V lighter socket in your car, attach the hose to the board, turn it on and away you go. Some pumps even have an automatic shut-off function, so you pre-set the PSI you want the paddleboard to inflate to and just let the pump do its thing. Once it hits the PSI you set, it turns off by itself. So no worries about forgetting you turned the pump on whilst you faff around, drink coffee and chat to friends (which I’ve done a few times).
What I love about having an electric paddleboard pump is whilst it’s inflating, you can get yourself ready, assess the conditions and not be knackered before you hit the water.
A word of warning
What I don’t love about electric sup pumps is the noise and it has somewhat split opinions within the paddleboarding community here in the UK. Sure they are easy, but they make a hell of a noise and if you are in a residential area, you can easily piss off the locals. This is especially the case if you want to do a sunrise SUP session at 6:30 am on a Sunday morning!
We’ve had a local paddleboard group shut down recently because residents complained about the noise whilst inflating the boards.
So if you want to use an electric sup pump, please be respectful of where you are using it. If you find you are trying to inflate the board first thing in a built-up area, maybe think twice and try a double chamber pump.

Along with our usual review of ease of use, quality and price, we also ran a head-to-head test to see what pump what the quickest and which one was the quietest. It was for us to see if there is much variation in the performance of these pumps, or are they just all very similar with a different plastic shell?
We used a Bluefin 12’ Cruise as the test board to inflate. The board is a large all-rounder that can withstand high pressures, so perfect to test these pumps with. For the time we simply used the stopwatch on our phone to record how long it took to get the Bluefin to 15PSI.
For the noise, we used an app called ‘Sound meter’ that records decibels using the mobile phone speaker. The test took place in a quiet area, so hopefully gives a good indication of the noise. We tried to simulate real-world conditions, like placing the pump on the pavement.
